20844-critical-miscellanies-vol-3-of-3-e:
Erasmus was a man of wide reading, yet not a scholar in the strict sense. John Morley borrows that verdict in his essay on Pattison's Memoirs, in Critical Miscellanies. Mark Pattison, an Oxford rector, left memoirs of a keen, questing mind.

Morley weighs Pattison's learning, doubt, and lonely search for truth. Oxford in ferment, church strife, and books fill the backdrop. The essay blends life study with literary judgment in Morley's crisp style. Readers who like Victorian essays at their most thoughtful will find a sharp mind judging a kindred one here.
34705-russian-fairy-tales-from-the-skazk:
Russian Fairy Tales holds tales drawn from the stores of Polevoi. R Nisbet Bain turned the tales into English for young readers. Drawings by an artist named Gere dress the text of the book. This copy is a third print, set in London in nineteen hundred and one.

The front note tells how a great hoard of folk tales fed the pick. A famed czar era scholar chose three dozen tales most fit for children. Those tales first came out at Saint Petersburg in eighteen seventy four. Bain notes that a prior book first taught Britain of the rich Slav lore. Bold old world turns and strong folk speech mark the tales inside.
44786-agent-nine-and-the-jewel-mystery-a:
Agent Nine and the Jewel Mystery was published in 1935. The Goldsmith Publishing Company issued it at Chicago. Graham Dean wrote the boys' detective story. Agent Nine's First Case stands as his earlier book. Its subtitle promises thrilling exploits of the G men. Thirty six chapters make the tale. An embarrassing situation opens it, and a new case follows. Tully's challenge and the Southern Limited come early. Papers vanish, and Bob gets a warning midway. Lights go out; a fight for life follows. Into angry waters and picking up clues fill the pursuit. Sheriff McCurdy talks at chapter twenty seven. Lost island ahead and a shanty stand near the end. Chapter one makes Bob Houston a full agent.

He steps from the Department of Justice Building a made man. His uncle, a famous detective, clasps him at the curb.
51708-tolstoi-for-the-young-select-tales:
Mrs R S Townsend translated Tolstoi for the Young, select tales from Tolstoi, issued in London in nineteen sixteen. Kegan Paul published it, with Dutton in New York. Michel Sevier painted six coloured plates. Ivan the Fool fronts the set as its first and longest tale.

Where There Is Love, There Is God Also follows in the contents. A Prisoner, from the Caucasus, and Emelian and the Empty Drum come next. Three Questions and The Godson close the small shelf. Ivan's tale opens on a rich peasant with three sons. Simon the Warrior and Taras the Pot-bellied stand beside the fool. Tolstoi wrote these tales for Russian peasants; Townsend carries them to English children.
52402-the-princess-pourquoi:
The Princess Pourquoi gathers five fairy tales by Margaret Sherwood, printed at Boston and New York in 1907. Three of them first appeared in Scribner's Magazine. The others ran in the Atlantic Monthly and McClure's. Pictures fill the book, starting with the princess whose big eyes grew wiser every day.

The title tale opens in a country very far away, where a new princess is born. Her parents hold a great christening feast for crowned heads and fairies. In the middle of the rite, as custom demands, a very angry guest arrives. The other tales treat a clever necromancer, a princess and a microbe, and seven studious sisters. Sherwood writes old fairy forms with a modern wink.
55284-reminiscences-of-leo-nicolayevitch:
Reminiscences of Leo Nicolayevitch Tolstoi, by Maxim Gorky, is a memoir of the great Russian novelist in his last years. The hosted copy is the second edition from the Hogarth Press, 1920, in the authorized English version by Koteliansky and Leonard Woolf. Notes written in the Crimea in 1900 and 1901 form the first half.

Gorky watches Tolstoi think about God, illness, and pride with a novelist's eye for the telling detail, down to his knotted, gifted hands. A letter of 1910, written after Tolstoi fled his home and died, closes the book. It remains one of the closest portraits of Tolstoi ever made.
65159-talks-with-tolstoi:
Goldenveizer kept a diary of his friendship of nearly fifteen years with Leo Tolstoi. Talks with Tolstoi, published in London in 1923, was translated by Koteliansky and Virginia Woolf. Goldenveizer was a Russian musician who first visited Tolstoi's house in January 1896, before he was twenty-one. He wrote down Tolstoi's words and the events of his private life.

The translator's note says this selection comes from the first volume of the diary, printed at Moscow in late 1922. Records grow fuller after 1908 and fullest in 1910, the last year of Tolstoi's life. Goldenveizer calls the diary a document, not literature. Readers hear a great writer talking at home, day by day, in his final years.
67151-the-proofs-of-christ-s-resurrectio:
Charles R Morrison wrote The Proofs of Christ's Resurrection, published at Andover in 1882 by Warren F Draper. Morrison treats the resurrection as a question of evidence. His subtitle says the argument runs from a lawyer's standpoint. He quotes Professor Greenleaf, the great writer on evidence, to urge lawyers to study the case.

Morrison says everything in Christian faith hinges on this one question. His book offers a compact, careful statement of the historical facts. It tests the honesty and soundness of the New Testament writings. He borrows from other scholars where they are strong, and credits them. Yet he claims to form his own judgment from all sources at hand. The book is a courtroom-style brief for a church doctrine.
britannica-1911-adenes-le-roi:
Adenes le Roi, a French trouvere born in Brabant about 1240, has a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He owed his education to the kindness of Henry the Third, duke of Brabant. He stayed in favour at court for some time after the death of his patron in 1261. In 1269 he entered the service of Guy de Dampierre, later count of Flanders.

Adenes in all likelihood served Guy as king of the minstrels at his court. In 1270 he followed Guy on the failed crusade to Tunis in which Louis the Ninth lost his life. The party came home by way of Sicily and Italy on that voyage. Adenes left exact descriptions in his poems of the places they passed through. The purity of his French, free of local traits, points to a long residence in France.
britannica-1911-areoi:
Areoi, also called Areoiti, was a secret society that began in Tahiti and is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Its reach spread later to other islands of the South Pacific. Both sexes could join its ranks. At its core the group was one of faith.

Members called themselves kin of Oro-Tetifa, a Polynesian god. They fell into seven or more grades, each with its own tattoo marks. Chiefs held the top grade at once, while plain members rose only through entry rites. The Areoi held great privileges as keepers of knowledge. Folk saw them as go betweens for God and man and feared them as agents of the taboo. They could cast out those who broke its rules. Their chief aim was worship of the powers that give life.
britannica-1911-estrades-godefroi:
Godefroi, comte d'Estrades, a French envoy and marshal who lived from 1607 to 1686, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Agen, the son of a backer of Henry the Fourth. As a boy he served as page to Louis the Thirteenth. At nineteen he was sent on a mission to Holland.

The entry lists the great deals he helped to strike for France. He won back Dunkirk from England in 1662. He worked on the treaties of Breda and of Nijmwegen as well. He also fought in the chief wars of Louis the Fourteenth, in Italy, Spain, and Holland. In 1675 he was made a marshal of France. His letters from Holland were later printed in nine volumes.
britannica-1911-pakhoi:
Pakhoi is a place entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It describes a port town in China, on a bay of a gulf in the south. The town stands on a point of land in the west of its province. About twenty five thousand people lived there at the time.

The entry tells how a den of sea robbers grew into a trade port. Free of tax at first, it drew trade when war shut other routes. Steam ships from abroad began to call there in the late years of the century. Dried fish, sugar, oils, and hides form the chief goods sent out. A large junk trade links the town to Macao.
britannica-1911-songhoi:
Songhoi are a people of the middle Niger river in west Africa, introduced in a 1911 Britannica entry. They held a state of their own from the eighth to the sixteenth century. At their height they ruled Timbuktu and led the western Sudan in power. About two million of them remained, though their freedom as a nation was lost.

Where they came from was much disputed among writers of the age. Barth, their fullest student, held them native to the Niger vale yet sought links to Egypt. Their own tales place their first home to the east of the river. A Timbuktu history names their first king and opens the royal line.
doe-osti-3002982-a-latent-variable-formu:
Carlos Llosa-Vite, Daniel M. Dunlavy, and Richard B. Lehoucq of Sandia, with Oscar López and Arvind Prasadan, reframe a tensor model in report SAND2025-14005R. The model is the Poisson canonical polyadic tensor model, used for count data arranged in multiway tables. Their trick is a latent-variable view: the observed tensor is what remains after hiding one dimension of a larger random tensor.

From that view, the authors derive maximum-likelihood estimators for the model. They show that several well-known fitting algorithms for nonnegative matrix and tensor factorization are really expectation-maximization algorithms in disguise. They also derive the observed and expected Fisher information matrices. Those matrices reveal how tensor rank affects identifiability, whether the data can pin down the factors at all. Rank-one models simplify greatly.
doe-osti-3816540-statistical-correlation:
National Laboratory of the Rockies report NLR/TP-5700-101179, dated September 2026, links solar mirror aim errors to wind strength. Matthew Emes, Devon Kesseli, Matthew Neber, and Stephanie Meyen are the printed authors. Heliostats steer sunbeams onto a tower receiver, and wind pushes their facets off aim. Published field data on that drift are sparse. The team set a laser test at the lab's Flatirons Campus platform. A camera watched the beam spot wander on a grid target while gauges logged each gust.

Side-to-side drift grew with peak wind speed along a logarithmic curve. Up-and-down drift grew faster, along an exponential curve. Both also fit the square-of-speed curve expected from wind load physics. Which pattern rules depends on the mirror's frame design. Next steps call for more field runs to split gravity sag from wind push. The work sits inside the Heliostat Consortium's field task.
nasa-tm-19690019484-a-procedure-for-furn:
Thomas J. Moore and Donald W. Adams of Lewis Research Center wrote this June 1969 memorandum, TM X-1815. They give a procedure for joining tungsten-uranium dioxide cermet cylinders with furnace brazed butt joints, at three thousand degrees Celsius. Such heat-proof cylinders serve high-temperature nuclear work. The joint had to fill completely, with no defects and little excess braze metal.

Brazing in helium with a tungsten-osmium alloy joined the cylinder's lengthwise seam successfully, they report. The team also tried alloy placement methods, cylinder orientations, and two alternate alloys briefly. One cost appeared: the heat cycle cut the parent material's strength by about a fifth. Larger tungsten grains explain the loss, they judge, and a later heat treatment removed an unwanted phase from the braze.
podcast-dannyjones-DCenM4t7soI:
Decorated SEAL veteran Kristin Beck joins Danny Jones for KONCRETE number 59. Beck served over twenty years on three SEAL teams, including Team 6. She deployed thirteen times to Bosnia, Iraq, and Afghanistan.

Beck earned more than fifty ribbons across seven combat tours. The title names her later life as a transgender woman. Jones traces the path from elite warrior to public advocate. Beck speaks about duty, identity, and the cost of both lives. The episode offers a rare long talk with a soldier whose story crosses two worlds. Her candor makes the hour stand out.
